Part II · Semiconductor quantum dots · Chapter 6

Electrons in semiconductors: bands, heterostructures and 2DEGs

Why you need this

Before an electron can be trapped in a quantum dot, it must be confined to a thin sheet: a two-dimensional electron gas. How that sheet is made decides almost everything about your device: whether gates attract or repel electrons, how big the dots are, how much charge noise there is, whether there are nuclear spins, and, in silicon, the size of the troublesome "valley splitting". When a paper says "undoped Si/SiGe heterostructure, 2DEG 50 nm below the surface, mobility \(2\times10^5\) cm²/Vs", this chapter tells you what each of those words means for your experiment.

You know from solid-state physics that electrons in a crystal live in energy bands, and that a semiconductor has an empty conduction band above a full valence band with a gap in between. This chapter recalls the few results we need and then builds up to the layered structures used for quantum dots.

6.1Bands, effective mass and why electrons in a crystal look light

In a crystal, the electron's energy depends on its wave vector \(\vec k\). Near the bottom of the conduction band, at wave vector \(\vec k_0\), the energy is approximately parabolic:

\[ E(\vec k) \approx E_c + \frac{\hbar^2}{2}\sum_i \frac{(k_i - k_{0,i})^2}{m_i^*} . \]

The constants \(m_i^*\) are the effective masses. They absorb the whole effect of the periodic crystal potential: near the band edge, an electron behaves like a free particle with mass \(m^*\) instead of the free-electron mass \(m_e\). This is the effective-mass approximation, and it lets us treat a dot like a "particle in a box" with a modified mass.

PropertySiliconGaAs
Band gap at low T1.17 eV (indirect)1.52 eV (direct)
Conduction band minima6 equivalent "Δ valleys" along ⟨100⟩, at about 85% of the way to the zone edge1 minimum at the zone centre (Γ point)
Effective massanisotropic: \(m_l = 0.92\,m_e\) (along the valley axis), \(m_t = 0.19\,m_e\) (across)isotropic: \(0.067\,m_e\)
Relative permittivity \(\varepsilon_r\)11.712.9
Electron g-factor≈ 2.00 (weak spin–orbit)≈ −0.44 (stronger spin–orbit)
Nuclear spinsonly 29Si (4.7% natural), can be removedevery Ga and As nucleus (spin 3/2)

Values are standard textbook numbers; see the reviews for context [8, 18].

The light mass in GaAs makes quantum effects appear on larger length scales, so GaAs dots can be larger and easier to make. The heavier transverse mass in silicon means silicon dots must be smaller (tens of nanometres) for the same orbital energy spacing. The table's last two rows explain why silicon won the coherence race.

6.2Confinement in one direction: quantum wells and 2DEGs

If you confine an electron in the z direction to a layer of thickness \(w\), its z motion is quantised like a particle in a box, with energies \(E_n \approx \hbar^2\pi^2 n^2/(2m_z w^2)\), while it moves freely in x and y. If only the lowest z level (\(n=1\)) is occupied, the electrons form a two-dimensional electron gas (2DEG).

Two useful 2D results:

  • Density of states is constant: \(D = g_s g_v m^*/(2\pi\hbar^2)\) per unit area and energy, where \(g_s = 2\) is the spin degeneracy and \(g_v\) the valley degeneracy (2 for silicon wells, 1 for GaAs).
  • Electron density \(n\) is set by the gate voltage through a parallel-plate capacitor: \(n \approx C_{\text{gate}}(V_g - V_{\text{th}})/e\) per unit area, where \(V_{\text{th}}\) is the turn-on (threshold) voltage. Typical Si/SiGe quantum-dot wafers run at \(n \sim (1\text{–}5)\times 10^{11}\) cm⁻².

The quality of a 2DEG is usually quoted as its mobility \(\mu\) (drift velocity per unit electric field). High mobility means little disorder. Si/SiGe quantum-dot wafers reach \(10^5\)–\(10^6\) cm²/Vs; the best GaAs/AlGaAs wafers exceed \(10^7\) cm²/Vs. Mobility is measured in Hall bars on the same wafer, and labs also quote the percolation density: the lowest density at which the 2DEG still conducts. A low percolation density (around \(10^{10}\) cm⁻²) indicates a clean, quiet potential landscape, which is what quantum dots need.

6.3The Si/SiGe heterostructure

Germanium has a 4% larger lattice constant than silicon, and SiGe alloys lie in between. A heterostructure for electron spin qubits is grown like this (Figure 1.1):

  1. A silicon wafer, then a graded buffer in which the Ge fraction rises slowly to about 30% over a few micrometres. Defects from the lattice mismatch are trapped in this buffer.
  2. A thick relaxed Si0.7Ge0.3 layer with the larger lattice constant.
  3. A thin (about 10 nm) silicon quantum well. Because it is grown on the larger SiGe lattice, it is stretched in-plane: tensile strain.
  4. A SiGe spacer (30–50 nm), a thin Si cap, an oxide, and the metal gates.

The strain is essential. In bulk silicon all six Δ valleys have the same energy. Tensile in-plane strain lowers the two valleys whose axis points out of the plane (along ±z) by roughly 100–200 meV relative to the four in-plane valleys. The conduction band in the silicon layer is also lower than in the SiGe around it by roughly 150 meV, so electrons collect in the silicon well. In those two z valleys, the in-plane effective mass is the light transverse mass \(m_t = 0.19\,m_e\), which helps make reasonably sized dots [8].

Undoped, accumulation-mode devices

Modern Si/SiGe qubit wafers are undoped. With no gate voltage there are no free electrons near the well. Positive voltages on accumulation gates pull electrons in from implanted ohmic contacts to form reservoirs, and positive plunger gates pull electrons into the dots. Without dopant atoms nearby, the potential is quieter. The price is that you need a dense set of gates to make anything happen, usually in several overlapping layers of aluminium or palladium separated by thin oxide. Overlapping-gate designs, introduced for Si/SiGe by the Princeton group, let every barrier and plunger be controlled independently [7].

6.4Valleys: silicon's extra quantum number

The two lowest valleys (+z and −z) are degenerate in the ideal strained well. Electrons in a dot then have an extra two-fold degree of freedom, the valley, besides spin. A sharp interface couples the two valleys and splits them into two states separated by the valley splitting \(E_{VS}\).

Why it matters for spin qubits:

  • If \(E_{VS}\) is smaller than or comparable to the Zeeman energy, a "spin-up, lower valley" state can be close in energy to "spin-down, upper valley". These states mix via spin–orbit coupling and T1 collapses (the relaxation hot spot).
  • Pauli spin blockade readout (Chapter 11) relies on the two-electron triplet states being high in energy. A small valley splitting provides a low-energy triplet-like state that lifts the blockade and ruins readout.
  • Small valley splittings also make it hard to shuttle electrons between dots without errors.

In Si/SiGe, \(E_{VS}\) is typically 20–300 µeV and varies from dot to dot, because the random arrangement of Ge atoms at the interface (alloy disorder) shifts the valley coupling. Measuring it on each dot is part of device characterisation, by spectroscopy, by finding the T1 hot spot versus magnetic field, or by magnetospectroscopy [7]. Si-MOS devices, with a sharp Si/SiO2 interface, usually have larger valley splittings (0.1–1 meV) but more disorder [8]. GaAs has a single conduction-band minimum and no valley problem.

Worked example

A dot has \(E_{VS} = 60\ \mu\)eV. At what field does the spin Zeeman energy reach the valley splitting (the hot spot)?

\(E_Z = g\mu_B B = 2\times57.9\ \mu\text{eV/T}\times B\). Setting \(E_Z = 60\ \mu\)eV gives \(B = 0.52\) T, a qubit frequency of about 14.5 GHz. Operating near 0.5 T would make T1 short. You would choose a field well below (say 0.3 T, 8.4 GHz) or, if possible, well above. Notice that the field you choose also decides your microwave hardware (Chapter 2).

6.5GaAs/AlGaAs heterostructures

In the classic GaAs system, a layer of AlGaAs (larger band gap) sits on GaAs. Silicon donor atoms placed in the AlGaAs, away from the interface ("modulation doping"), give up their electrons, which fall into a triangular well at the GaAs side of the interface and form a 2DEG about 50–100 nm below the surface. The donors stay behind, far from the electrons, so mobility is very high. Here the 2DEG exists without any gate voltage. Negative voltages on surface gates deplete the electrons underneath, and dots are defined as small islands left between depleted regions. That is why older GaAs papers show gate patterns that look like fingers pinching off a channel [18].

GaAs remains valuable for spin physics because its devices are easy to make and tune, and because some experiments benefit from its strong hyperfine interaction or spin–orbit coupling. Its weakness for qubits is the nuclear-spin bath, which limits \(T_2^*\) to about 10 ns without special techniques.

6.6Other platforms you will read about

  • Si-MOS: electrons at a Si/SiO2 interface under aluminium gates, close to standard transistor technology. Larger valley splitting, more interface disorder.
  • Holes in Ge/SiGe: planar germanium quantum wells host holes with a light in-plane mass, strong spin–orbit coupling (allowing all-electrical driving without a micromagnet) and low hyperfine coupling. Four-qubit processors have been made in this system [12].
  • Donors in silicon: a single phosphorus atom provides both an electron spin and a nuclear spin qubit.
  • Fin and nanowire devices (FinFET, CMOS foundry qubits), in which the dot forms at the corner of a silicon channel.

The measurement techniques in this book apply to all of them. The details of tuning differ.

In the lab

Before a new wafer is used for qubits, groups measure Hall bars at 4 K or below to get density and mobility versus gate voltage, then measure single-electron transistors to check charge noise. Only promising wafers go on to full qubit devices. Ask about the heterostructure details whenever you get a new device: spacer thickness (deeper 2DEG means quieter but less strongly controlled dots), well width, and the isotope content of the well (28Si purified or natural).

Check yourself

1. Why do gates on undoped Si/SiGe need positive voltages, while gates on modulation-doped GaAs use negative voltages?

Show answer
Undoped Si/SiGe has no free electrons in the well until a positive gate voltage pulls them in (accumulation mode). Doped GaAs already has a 2DEG; negative gate voltages push electrons away (depletion mode) to define dots.

2. What two roles does tensile strain play in a Si quantum well?

Show answer
It lowers the two out-of-plane (±z) valleys well below the four in-plane valleys, leaving just a two-fold valley degeneracy, and it gives the light transverse mass for in-plane motion. (Together with the band offset it also confines electrons in the silicon layer.)

3. A paper reports a valley splitting of 25 µeV in one dot. Name two problems this might cause.

Show answer
A spin–valley relaxation hot spot at a low field (about 0.22 T), limiting T1 and the usable field range; and weak Pauli spin blockade, because a low-lying excited valley state allows triplets to tunnel, reducing readout fidelity.
Summary
  • Near the band edge, electrons act as particles with an effective mass: \(0.19\,m_e\) (in-plane, strained Si) or \(0.067\,m_e\) (GaAs).
  • Heterostructures confine electrons into 2DEGs. Undoped Si/SiGe works in accumulation mode with positive gates; doped GaAs works in depletion mode with negative gates.
  • Silicon has two low valleys separated by a device-dependent valley splitting (20–300 µeV in Si/SiGe), which limits T1 and readout if small.
  • Silicon's nuclear-spin bath can be removed by isotopic purification; GaAs's cannot.

Part II · Semiconductor quantum dots · Chapter 7

Making a quantum dot: Coulomb blockade and the constant-interaction model

Why you need this

The first measurements on any quantum-dot device are Coulomb peaks and Coulomb diamonds. They prove a dot has formed, tell you its charging energy, and give you the lever arm: the conversion factor between millivolts on a gate and micro-electronvolts in the dot. You need that number for everything after: converting pulse amplitudes from the RFSoC into energies, calibrating detuning axes, and comparing your device with papers. This chapter derives the simple model that every group uses.

A quantum dot is a tiny island of electrons connected to the outside world by tunnel barriers. Because the island is so small, adding even one electron costs a noticeable amount of energy. At low temperature that cost stops electrons from flowing, except at special gate voltages. That effect, Coulomb blockade, is what lets us count and control electrons one at a time.

7.1The picture: an island with toll gates

Think of the dot as a small parking garage between two big car parks (the source and drain reservoirs). Each entrance has a narrow tunnel (the barrier). The garage is so small that each car already inside makes it noticeably harder to squeeze another one in. A gate electrode nearby acts like a pump that changes how attractive the garage is. Cars only flow through when the cost of entering from the source is low enough and the cost of leaving to the drain is low enough. For most gate settings, they get stuck: the garage holds a fixed number \(N\) of cars and nothing flows. Only at specific gate settings does the count alternate between \(N\) and \(N+1\), letting cars pass one by one.

7.2Two conditions for Coulomb blockade

Blockade needs two things [23]:

  1. Large charging energy compared with temperature. Adding one electron to an island of total capacitance \(C_\Sigma\) costs about \(E_C = e^2/C_\Sigma\). This must exceed \(k_BT\). For a disc-shaped dot of radius \(r\) in a medium of permittivity \(\varepsilon\), \(C \approx 8\varepsilon r\). With \(r = 30\) nm in silicon, \(C\approx 8\times 11.7\times 8.85\times10^{-12}\times 30\times10^{-9} \approx 2.5\times10^{-17}\) F, so \(E_C \approx 6\) meV. Nearby metal gates add capacitance and reduce this; measured values in Si/SiGe dots are typically 2–10 meV, far above \(k_BT \approx 10\ \mu\)eV.
  2. Opaque tunnel barriers. The tunnel resistance must exceed the resistance quantum \(h/e^2 \approx 25.8\) kΩ. Otherwise quantum fluctuations of the electron number (the uncertainty principle applied to energy and the time an electron stays on the dot) wash out the discrete charge.

7.3The constant-interaction model

The constant-interaction (CI) model makes two assumptions: all Coulomb interactions are described by a single constant capacitance \(C_\Sigma\), and the single-particle levels \(E_n\) do not depend on how many electrons there are. The total energy of the dot with \(N\) electrons is then

\[ U(N) = \frac{\big[-e(N - N_0) + C_S V_S + C_D V_D + C_G V_G\big]^2}{2C_\Sigma} + \sum_{n=1}^{N} E_n , \]

where \(N_0\) is a constant offset from background charges. The first term is the classical electrostatic energy of a charged capacitor; the second is the quantum energy of the occupied orbitals.

What matters for transport is not \(U(N)\) itself but the energy needed to add the \(N\)th electron, the electrochemical potential

\[ \mu(N) = U(N) - U(N-1) = \Big(N - N_0 - \tfrac12\Big)E_C - \frac{E_C}{e}\big(C_S V_S + C_D V_D + C_G V_G\big) + E_N . \]

Two features of this formula are the keys to every measurement:

  • Gate voltage shifts all levels linearly. \(\partial\mu/\partial V_G = -e\,C_G/C_\Sigma\). The dimensionless ratio
\[ \alpha_G = \frac{C_G}{C_\Sigma} \]

is the lever arm of the gate. A 1 mV change on the gate moves the dot's levels by \(\alpha_G\) meV. Typical plunger lever arms are 0.05–0.2 eV/V in Si/SiGe.

  • Levels are spaced by the addition energy.
\[ E_{\text{add}}(N) = \mu(N+1) - \mu(N) = E_C + \Delta E , \]

where \(\Delta E = E_{N+1} - E_N\) is the orbital (or valley) spacing, zero if the next electron goes into the same orbital with opposite spin. For the first few electrons in a silicon dot, \(\Delta E\) includes the valley splitting and the orbital energy, so addition energies vary from electron to electron. This "shell filling" pattern is a fingerprint of the few-electron regime.

7.4Coulomb peaks: transport at small bias

Apply a tiny bias between source and drain so that \(\mu_S \gtrsim \mu_D\). An electron can pass through the dot only if some \(\mu(N)\) lies between them: it tunnels in from the source (the dot goes from \(N-1\) to \(N\)) and then out to the drain (back to \(N-1\)). Otherwise the electron number is fixed and no current flows. Sweeping the plunger voltage moves the ladder of \(\mu(N)\) through the bias window, so conductance appears as a series of sharp Coulomb peaks.

At low bias and with weak tunnel coupling, the line shape of a single peak is set by the Fermi distribution of the reservoirs [23]:

\[ G(V_G) \propto \cosh^{-2}\!\Big(\frac{e\alpha_G (V_G - V_0)}{2k_B T_e}\Big) . \]

Its full width at half maximum is \(3.5\,k_BT_e/(e\alpha_G)\). If you know the lever arm, the peak width gives the electron temperature \(T_e\), a sensitive test of how well your wiring filters noise (Chapter 16).

Worked example: electron temperature

A Coulomb peak has a full width at half maximum of 0.25 mV in plunger voltage. The lever arm (from diamonds, below) is 0.1 eV/V. Then \(3.5\,k_BT_e = 0.1\times 0.25\ \text{meV} = 25\ \mu\)eV, so \(k_BT_e = 7.1\ \mu\)eV and \(T_e = 7.1/86 \approx 83\) mK. If the fridge reads 15 mK, your electrons are hotter than the fridge, which is normal. If you get 300 mK, look for missing filters or noisy instruments.

7.5Coulomb diamonds: bias spectroscopy

Now sweep both the plunger voltage and the source–drain bias \(V_{SD}\). Current is blocked inside diamond-shaped regions where no level fits into the bias window. Each diamond corresponds to a fixed electron number.

Reading a diamond is a standard skill:

  • Height. The diamond's tips in \(V_{SD}\) are at \(\pm E_{\text{add}}/e\). This gives the addition energy directly in meV, without knowing any capacitance.
  • Width. The diamond's width along \(V_G\) is \(\Delta V_G = E_{\text{add}}/(e\alpha_G)\). Dividing height by width gives the lever arm: \(\alpha_G = (E_{\text{add}}/e)/\Delta V_G\).
  • Slopes. The two edge slopes give the ratios \(C_G/(C_G + C_S)\) and \(C_G/C_D\), from which all three capacitances follow.
  • Excited states. Lines inside the conducting region, parallel to the diamond edges, mark the onset of transport through excited orbital, valley or spin states. Their position in \(V_{SD}\) is their excitation energy.
Worked example: lever arm from a diamond

A diamond reaches \(V_{SD} = \pm 4.2\) mV at its tips and is 35 mV wide in plunger voltage. Then \(E_{\text{add}} = 4.2\) meV and \(\alpha = 4.2/35 = 0.12\) eV/V. Now you can convert anything: a 2 mV pulse on this plunger shifts the dot's energy by 240 µeV, which is about 58 GHz in frequency units (1 µeV ≈ 0.242 GHz). This conversion is used constantly when designing pulse sequences.

In the lab

In modern qubit devices with many gates, groups often do not measure diamonds through the qubit dot itself, because the dots are tuned to have very opaque barriers and the current is too small to measure. Instead they measure diamonds on the sensor dot (Chapter 9), and for qubit dots they measure the lever arm using photon-assisted tunnelling (a microwave on a gate produces side-peaks spaced by \(hf/(e\alpha)\)) or using the thermal broadening of charge transitions with a known temperature [7].

7.6The few-electron regime

Spin qubits normally use a dot holding exactly one electron (or, for some encodings, one or three). To know you have exactly one, you must see the last transition, after which no more charge transitions occur as you make the plunger more negative. In transport this is hard because tunnel rates drop as the dot empties; it is much easier with a charge sensor, which does not need current through the qubit dot. Chapter 9 explains charge sensing, and Chapter 15 describes how groups reach the single-electron regime in practice.

On the 4x2

Coulomb peaks and diamonds are DC measurements: bias voltages and slow gate sweeps, read with a current amplifier or a lock-in. The 4x2's balun-coupled ports cannot provide the DC bias or measure DC current, so these first measurements are done with DC sources and a lock-in amplifier. Where the 4x2 becomes useful is the next step: charge sensing with RF reflectometry, which is fast enough to map charge states in milliseconds instead of minutes (Chapters 9 and 39). Note that the on-board baluns are rated from 10 MHz [2], so "lock-in" style excitation at kHz frequencies will not pass through them.

Check yourself

1. Two neighbouring Coulomb peaks are 22 mV apart and the next pair 30 mV apart. The lever arm is 0.1 eV/V. What are the addition energies, and what might explain the difference?

Show answer
\(E_{\text{add}} = 2.2\) meV and 3.0 meV. The extra 0.8 meV in the second case is the orbital or valley spacing \(\Delta E\): the corresponding electron had to occupy a new, higher state rather than the same orbital with opposite spin.

2. Why must the tunnel resistances exceed about 26 kΩ?

Show answer
The energy uncertainty of an electron that spends a time \(RC\) on the dot is about \(h/(RC)\). It must be smaller than the charging energy \(e^2/C\), giving \(R \gg h/e^2\). Otherwise the electron number is not well defined.

3. You change the plunger by +3 mV and the lever arm is 0.08. By how much did the dot's levels move, in µeV and in GHz?

Show answer
\(0.08 \times 3\) meV = 240 µeV ≈ 58 GHz (using 1 µeV ≈ 0.242 GHz).
Summary
  • Coulomb blockade needs \(E_C = e^2/C_\Sigma \gg k_BT\) and tunnel resistances \(\gg h/e^2\).
  • In the constant-interaction model, the electrochemical potential \(\mu(N)\) shifts linearly with gate voltage via the lever arm \(\alpha = C_G/C_\Sigma\), and consecutive levels are spaced by \(E_{\text{add}} = E_C + \Delta E\).
  • Coulomb peaks mark charge transitions; their width gives the electron temperature.
  • Coulomb diamonds give \(E_{\text{add}}\) (height), the lever arm (height/width) and excited-state energies.
  • These DC measurements use DC instruments; the 4x2 enters with RF charge sensing.

Part II · Semiconductor quantum dots · Chapter 8

Double and multiple dots: charge stability diagrams and virtual gates

Why you need this

Every spin-qubit experiment happens inside a charge stability diagram: a 2D map of which charge configuration the dots are in as you vary two gate voltages. Readout points, initialisation points, manipulation points and exchange pulses are all defined as positions in this map. You will spend more time looking at these maps than at any other kind of plot, and making them fast is one of the best uses of an RFSoC. This chapter explains where their honeycomb pattern comes from, what the interdot transition is, and how virtual gates make the map easy to navigate.

8.1Two dots, two gates, many capacitances

Put two dots side by side, each with its own plunger gate (P1, P2), separated by a barrier gate that controls tunnelling between them. In the constant-interaction picture, three energies describe the electrostatics [24]:

  • \(E_{C1}\) and \(E_{C2}\): the charging energies of each dot.
  • \(E_{Cm}\): the mutual charging energy, the extra cost of adding an electron to one dot because of an electron on the other. It comes from the interdot capacitance \(C_m\).

Each plunger couples mostly to its own dot but also somewhat to the other: the lever-arm matrix

\[ \begin{pmatrix} \delta\mu_1 \\ \delta\mu_2 \end{pmatrix} = -e\begin{pmatrix} \alpha_{11} & \alpha_{12} \\ \alpha_{21} & \alpha_{22} \end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix} \delta V_{P1} \\ \delta V_{P2} \end{pmatrix} \]

has off-diagonal elements \(\alpha_{12}, \alpha_{21}\) called cross-capacitance (or crosstalk), typically 20–60% of the diagonal ones in dense Si/SiGe devices. A compact way to write the energy of the configuration \((N_1, N_2)\) is

\[ E(N_1,N_2) = \tfrac12 E_{C1}(N_1 - n_1)^2 + \tfrac12 E_{C2}(N_2 - n_2)^2 + E_{Cm}(N_1-n_1)(N_2-n_2), \]

where \(n_1, n_2\) are the (continuous) "gate-induced charges", linear combinations of the plunger voltages. At each gate voltage the system sits in the configuration with the lowest energy.

8.2The charge stability diagram

Plot the ground-state configuration over the \((V_{P1}, V_{P2})\) plane, and draw lines where it changes. The result is the famous honeycomb pattern of a charge stability diagram (CSD).

Learn to read the diagram's features:

  • Nearly vertical lines: the electron number on dot 1 changes (dot 1 exchanges an electron with its reservoir). They are not perfectly vertical because P2 also couples to dot 1.
  • Nearly horizontal lines: dot 2 changes.
  • Short diagonal segments: interdot transitions, e.g. (1,0)↔(0,1). The total electron number is constant, so in transport no current flows here, but a charge sensor sees the electron move.
  • Triple points: the ends of each interdot segment, where three configurations are degenerate. In transport, current only flows near triple points.
  • The length of the interdot segment is set by the mutual charging energy. If \(E_{Cm} = 0\), the segments shrink to points and the pattern becomes a square grid (two independent dots). If the dots merge into one, the lines become parallel diagonals.

Spin qubits usually work at the lowest charge cells: \((1,1)\) for two single-spin qubits, the boundary between \((1,1)\) and \((0,2)\) or \((2,0)\) for readout and singlet–triplet qubits. To be sure of the absolute numbers you must find the \((0,0)\) cell, beyond which no more lines appear.

8.3The interdot transition: a charge qubit

Zoom in on a single interdot transition, say between \((1,0)\) and \((0,1)\). One electron is shared between two dots. Define the detuning \(\varepsilon\) as the energy difference between the two configurations: \(\varepsilon < 0\) means the electron prefers the left dot, \(\varepsilon > 0\) the right. If the barrier lets the electron tunnel with amplitude \(t_c\) (the tunnel coupling), the two configurations form a two-level system:

\[ H = \frac{\varepsilon}{2}\,\tau_z + t_c\,\tau_x , \qquad E_\pm = \pm\frac12\sqrt{\varepsilon^2 + 4t_c^2}, \]

where the Pauli matrices \(\tau\) act on "left/right" instead of spin. This is exactly the qubit of Chapter 2, with charge instead of spin. At \(\varepsilon = 0\) the eigenstates are bonding and antibonding combinations of left and right, separated by \(2t_c\).

Tunnel coupling depends exponentially on the barrier gate voltage, typically changing by a factor of 10 for tens of millivolts. This exponential control is central to exchange-based gates (Chapter 14). You can measure \(t_c\) from how sharp the interdot transition looks in the charge sensor: the probability of finding the electron on the right goes from 0 to 1 over a detuning range of a few \(t_c\) (or a few \(k_BT_e\), whichever is larger). The thermal-equilibrium expression is

\[ P_R(\varepsilon) = \frac12\Big[1 + \frac{\varepsilon}{\sqrt{\varepsilon^2+4t_c^2}}\tanh\Big(\frac{\sqrt{\varepsilon^2+4t_c^2}}{2k_BT_e}\Big)\Big]. \]

Fitting this to a slow scan across the transition gives \(t_c\), provided you know the lever arm of the detuning axis.

Worked example: detuning in gate voltage

Detuning is usually swept by moving P1 and P2 in opposite directions along the axis perpendicular to the interdot line. If the lever arms are \(\alpha_{11} = \alpha_{22} = 0.1\) and crosstalk \(\alpha_{12} = \alpha_{21} = 0.03\), then changing \(V_{P1}\) by \(+\delta\) and \(V_{P2}\) by \(-\delta\) changes \(\mu_1 - \mu_2\) by \(-e(0.1 - 0.03 + 0.1 - 0.03)\delta = -0.14\,e\delta\). So 1 mV of this combined step moves the detuning by 140 µeV. To cross a transition with \(2t_c = 20\ \mu\)eV you need only about 0.15 mV of resolution, which is why gate-voltage noise must be in the µV range.

8.4Virtual gates

Because every gate affects every dot, tuning one parameter with physical gates moves all the others. The solution, now universal in multi-dot work, is to define virtual gates: linear combinations of physical gates that each act on only one dot [25, 26]. If the lever-arm matrix is \(A\) (normalised so its diagonal is 1), define

\[ \vec V' = A\,\vec V \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad \vec V = A^{-1}\vec V' . \]

Now changing \(V'_1\) changes only \(\mu_1\). In the \((V'_1, V'_2)\) plane, the dot-1 transitions are exactly vertical and the dot-2 transitions exactly horizontal.

To find \(A\), measure the slopes of the transition lines in a CSD. For a dot-1 line, \(\delta\mu_1 = 0\) along the line, so its slope is \(dV_{P2}/dV_{P1} = -\alpha_{11}/\alpha_{12}\). Do the same for dot-2 lines. The same idea extends to barrier gates: virtual barriers change one tunnel coupling while compensating the plungers so that the dots' energies stay fixed. In large arrays, groups calibrate matrices of 10×10 or more, often automatically [27].

On the 4x2

Virtual gates matter in two places in hardware:

  • DC sources. The slow gate voltages are set in virtual coordinates by your Python code, which converts them to physical voltages before sending them to the DC source.
  • Fast pulses. A fast pulse "on virtual plunger 1" really means playing scaled copies of a waveform on several physical gates at the same time. The HRL spinQICK firmware does this in real time with a crosstalk-compensation matrix in FPGA logic (11×11 on a ZCU216) [11]. The 4x2 has only two DAC outputs, so with it you can pulse at most two gates, for example P1 and P2 of a double dot. That is exactly what a detuning pulse needs. You compute the two waveforms in Python from the virtual-gate matrix and play them simultaneously on the two generators.

8.5Beyond two dots

Triple dots host exchange-only qubits (Chapter 13). Linear arrays of 4–12 dots host multi-qubit processors [16], and 2D arrays (2×2, 3×3 and larger) are under active development, especially in germanium. Their CSDs are high-dimensional, so groups take 2D slices along chosen virtual axes. Automated tuning methods, including machine-learning classifiers that recognise the charge configuration from an image of a CSD, are reviewed by Zwolak and Taylor [27]. Every one of those methods needs many CSD images, quickly, which is where fast RF readout and FPGA control pay off.

Check yourself

1. In a CSD, the dot-1 lines have slope \(-4\) and the dot-2 lines have slope \(-0.25\) (in \(dV_{P2}/dV_{P1}\)). Find the normalised lever-arm matrix.

Show answer
For dot-1 lines, slope \(= -\alpha_{11}/\alpha_{12} = -4\), so \(\alpha_{12}/\alpha_{11} = 0.25\). For dot-2 lines, \(\delta\mu_2 = 0\) gives slope \(= -\alpha_{21}/\alpha_{22} = -0.25\), so \(\alpha_{21}/\alpha_{22} = 0.25\). Normalised: \(A = \begin{pmatrix}1 & 0.25\\ 0.25 & 1\end{pmatrix}\).

2. Why does no transport current flow at an interdot transition (away from the triple points), although a charge sensor sees a clear signal?

Show answer
The total number of electrons is fixed there; an electron only moves between the dots and cannot pass from source to drain. A charge sensor detects the change in charge distribution regardless of current.

3. What happens to the honeycomb if the mutual charging energy goes to zero? If the dots merge?

Show answer
With \(E_{Cm} = 0\) the interdot segments vanish and the pattern becomes a grid of independent vertical and horizontal lines. If the dots merge into one large dot, both gates control the same island and the lines become parallel diagonals.
Summary
  • A double dot's charge configuration versus two gate voltages forms a honeycomb charge stability diagram; cells are labelled \((N_1,N_2)\).
  • Interdot transitions keep the total charge fixed; near them the electron forms a charge two-level system with gap \(2t_c\) at zero detuning.
  • Tunnel coupling depends exponentially on barrier voltage.
  • Virtual gates, built from the measured lever-arm matrix, give each axis control of one dot; fast virtual pulses require simultaneous scaled pulses on several gates.
PreviousChapter 7 · Making a quantum dot: Coulomb blockade and the constant-interaction modelNextChapter 9 · Charge sensing and RF reflectometry

Part II · Semiconductor quantum dots · Chapter 9

Charge sensing and RF reflectometry

Why you need this

Spin readout is charge readout in disguise: the spin state is converted into "did an electron move or not?" (Chapter 11), and that question is answered by a charge sensor. How fast and how cleanly you can read the sensor decides your readout fidelity, how quickly you can map charge stability diagrams, and how long every experiment takes. RF reflectometry is the standard fast technique, and it is the job the RFSoC 4x2 is best suited for: a carrier of a few hundred MHz out of a DAC, a reflected signal into an ADC, and real-time demodulation in the FPGA in between.

9.1Why sense charge instead of measuring current?

Measuring current through the qubit dots themselves has two problems. First, qubit dots are tuned with very opaque barriers so that electrons stay put; the currents would be femtoamperes. Second, a current means electrons passing through, which destroys the state you want to measure. A charge sensor avoids both: it is a separate, nearby conductor whose conductance depends on the electrostatic environment, so it detects charges in the qubit dots without any current flowing through them.

9.2The two kinds of charge sensor

  • Quantum point contact (QPC). A narrow constriction in the 2DEG, defined by two gates. Its conductance is quantised in steps of \(2e^2/h\); on the slope between steps, it is very sensitive to nearby charges. QPCs were the standard sensor in GaAs.
  • Sensor dot (single-electron transistor, SET). A larger quantum dot with relatively open barriers, tuned to the flank of one of its Coulomb peaks. A single electron arriving in a nearby qubit dot shifts the sensor's peak by a fraction of its width, changing the conductance by a large fraction. Sensor dots are standard in silicon devices.

The signal is the conductance change \(\Delta G\). The noise comes from the amplifier chain and from charge noise moving the sensor peak. The ratio, integrated over a measurement time, gives the readout SNR of Chapter 5.

9.3Why DC sensing is slow

The simplest way to read a sensor is to apply a small DC bias and measure the current with a room-temperature current amplifier. The problem is the wiring. A sensor with resistance \(R\sim 100\) kΩ connected through a coaxial cable to room temperature sees the cable's capacitance \(C_{\text{line}}\sim 100\) pF–1 nF. The resulting RC time constant is \(10^5\times 10^{-10} = 10\ \mu\)s or longer, and the current amplifier's own bandwidth (typically 1–100 kHz at high gain) limits things further. DC readout therefore needs tens of microseconds to milliseconds per point. That is fine for slow tune-up but slow for single-shot readout and very slow for mapping large CSDs.

9.4RF reflectometry: the idea

Instead of measuring a current, RF reflectometry measures how much of a radio-frequency wave is reflected from the sensor. The sensor is placed in an LC resonant circuit, so that its resistance changes the circuit's impedance. A carrier wave at the resonance frequency (typically 100 MHz–1 GHz) travels down a 50 Ω coaxial line to the circuit and reflects back. The reflected amplitude and phase depend on the sensor resistance. The cable capacitance no longer matters, because the cable is a transmission line with a defined impedance, not a lumped capacitor. Bandwidths of several MHz become possible [28, 29].

Analogy

Shout into a long pipe that ends at a wall: the echo comes back loud. If the pipe ends in open air, the echo is also strong (with opposite sign). If the pipe ends in a perfectly absorbing foam, no echo returns. The sensor plus resonator is a "foam" whose absorption changes with the sensor resistance. You listen to the echo's strength and timing to learn the resistance.

Reflection from a load

A wave travelling on a transmission line of characteristic impedance \(Z_0\) (50 Ω for standard coax) that meets a load of impedance \(Z\) is partly reflected. The reflection coefficient is [30]

\[ \Gamma = \frac{Z - Z_0}{Z + Z_0} . \]

If \(Z = Z_0\) (matched), \(\Gamma = 0\): all power is absorbed. If \(Z = 0\) (short) or \(Z = \infty\) (open), \(|\Gamma| = 1\): everything reflects. A sensor resistance of 100 kΩ on its own is so far from 50 Ω that it reflects almost everything, regardless of small changes. The resonator's job is to transform the sensor's large resistance into something close to 50 Ω, so that small changes in \(R\) produce large changes in \(\Gamma\).

The LC tank circuit

The load impedance seen from the line is

\[ Z(\omega) = i\omega L + \frac{1}{i\omega C_p + 1/R} . \]

For large \(R\), a short calculation (expand for \(\omega C_p R \gg 1\)) shows that near the resonance frequency

\[ f_0 = \frac{1}{2\pi\sqrt{LC_p}} \]

the circuit behaves like a resistance \(R_{\text{eff}} \approx L/(C_pR)\). Matching, \(R_{\text{eff}} = Z_0\), happens when the sensor resistance equals

\[ R_{\text{match}} = \frac{L}{Z_0 C_p} . \]

At matching \(|\Gamma| = 0\) at \(f_0\), and the sensitivity \(|d\Gamma/dR|\) is largest. Away from matching, the response is weaker.

Worked example: designing a tank

Your sensor dot, tuned to its most sensitive flank, has about 50 kΩ. Bond pads and PCB traces give \(C_p \approx 0.6\) pF. Which inductor matches it, and where is the resonance?

\(L = R_{\text{match}}Z_0C_p = 5\times10^4 \times 50 \times 0.6\times10^{-12} = 1.5\ \mu\)H. Then \(f_0 = 1/(2\pi\sqrt{1.5\times10^{-6}\times0.6\times10^{-12}}) = 168\) MHz. A real example: the Tohoku group used \(L = 1.2\ \mu\)H with \(C_p = 0.6\) pF, giving 193 MHz and matching at about 24 µS (42 kΩ), and noted that their device's actual conductance was far from this, which limited sensitivity [31]. This is the most common practical problem with reflectometry: the parasitic capacitance is not known until the device is cold, so the match is a guess. Variable capacitors (varactors) on the PCB allow tuning the match in situ.

9.5The measurement chain

Each part has a reason:

  • Attenuation on the way down removes thermal noise from warmer stages (Chapter 16) and sets the probe power at the device. Too much power heats the electrons and broadens the sensor peak; a common working point is around −90 to −110 dBm at the sample.
  • The directional coupler sends the incident wave through its weakly coupled port and the reflected wave out of its main port towards the amplifier, so the two are separated.
  • The cryogenic amplifier sets the noise floor. A HEMT amplifier at 4 K has a noise temperature of a few kelvin. Superconducting parametric amplifiers (JPAs, TWPAs) can approach the quantum limit and have improved spin readout speed significantly in some labs [29].
  • Demodulation multiplies the returning signal by the carrier (in-phase, I) and by a 90°-shifted copy (quadrature, Q), then low-pass filters. The result is a slowly varying complex number \(I + iQ \propto \Gamma\). With an RFSoC this happens digitally (Chapter 23).

How fast can you read?

For white amplifier noise, the SNR grows with integration time \(t\) as \(\sqrt t\). A useful figure of merit is the minimum integration time \(t_{\min}\) needed to reach SNR = 1; then SNR \(= \sqrt{t/t_{\min}}\). Good silicon sensor-dot reflectometry setups reach \(t_{\min}\) of order 10–100 ns with HEMT amplifiers, so SNR 6 (99.9% charge discrimination) takes a few microseconds. This is what enables single-shot spin readout in microseconds [32, 29].

9.6Gate-based (dispersive) sensing

An alternative attaches the resonator to a gate of the qubit dots rather than to a separate sensor. When an electron can tunnel back and forth near an interdot transition, it responds to the gate's RF voltage and adds a small quantum capacitance \(C_Q = (e\alpha)^2\,\partial P/\partial\varepsilon\). This shifts the resonance frequency, which appears as a phase shift of the reflected wave. Gate-based sensing needs no extra sensor dot, which is attractive for dense arrays and CMOS-style devices. Its signal is usually smaller than a well-tuned sensor dot's, and it only detects transitions where electrons can tunnel at the probe frequency [29].

9.7Frequency multiplexing

Several resonators with different inductors (different \(f_0\)) can share one input and one output line. Each sensor is probed by its own carrier tone, and the returning signal is demodulated at each tone separately. This "frequency multiplexing" reduces wiring, which is essential for larger devices. With an RFSoC, multiplexing is natural: one DAC can play the sum of several tones, and the FPGA can demodulate several frequencies from one ADC stream at once.

On the 4x2

Reflectometry is the 4x2's sweet spot:

  • Carriers of 100 MHz–1 GHz are deep inside the DACs' first Nyquist zone (up to about 4.9 GHz) and well above the baluns' 10 MHz lower limit [2].
  • QICK demodulates in the FPGA: a readout block multiplies the ADC data by its own numerically controlled oscillator, filters, decimates and accumulates over a programmable window, giving one I/Q pair per shot [9].
  • Generator and readout run from the same clock tree, so with QICK's frequency matching the demodulated phase is stable from shot to shot [4].
  • RFSoC-based reflectometry on gate-defined quantum dots has been demonstrated with QICK on a ZCU216 [31]. The same firmware concepts run on the 4x2.

What you still need outside the board: attenuators, a directional coupler, a cryogenic amplifier, a room-temperature amplifier and, usually, filters to keep DAC images and clock spurs out of the ADC. Chapter 39 builds this setup step by step.

Common mistake

Sending the DAC's full output power into the fridge. Even at −10 dBm out of the DAC, 0 dB of attenuation would deliver a signal around ten million times stronger than the −100 dBm a sensor dot wants, heating the electrons and saturating the amplifiers. Always calculate the power budget (Chapter 18) before connecting cables, and add attenuation first, remove it later.

Check yourself

1. Why does putting the sensor in an LC resonator make it fast, when the same cable used for DC readout made it slow?

Show answer
At DC the cable is a large lumped capacitance that must be charged through the sensor's high resistance (long RC time). At RF, a properly terminated coaxial cable is a transmission line with 50 Ω impedance; the resonator transforms the sensor's high resistance towards 50 Ω so changes in R appear as changes in reflection, with a bandwidth set by the resonator's quality factor (typically MHz).

2. \(C_p = 0.4\) pF and you want \(f_0 \approx 300\) MHz. Which inductor do you need, and what sensor resistance is matched?

Show answer
\(L = 1/((2\pi f_0)^2 C_p) = 1/((1.885\times10^9)^2\times 4\times10^{-13}) \approx 0.70\ \mu\)H. \(R_{\text{match}} = L/(Z_0C_p) = 7\times10^{-7}/(50\times4\times10^{-13}) = 35\) kΩ.

3. In blockade, the magnitude \(|\Gamma|\) barely changes with frequency. Why can you still detect a signal?

Show answer
The resonator is lossless at the device (\(R\to\infty\)), so all power is reflected, but the reflected phase still swings through the resonance. A small change in \(R\) or in capacitance (dispersive shift) changes the phase, which the I/Q demodulation detects.
Summary
  • Charge sensors (QPCs or sensor dots) detect electrons in nearby qubit dots without current through them.
  • DC readout is limited by cable capacitance to kHz bandwidths; RF reflectometry reaches MHz.
  • A tank circuit with \(f_0 = 1/(2\pi\sqrt{LC_p})\) transforms the sensor resistance; sensitivity peaks at \(R = L/(Z_0C_p)\).
  • The chain is: carrier → attenuators → directional coupler → tank → cryogenic amplifier → room-temperature amplifier → digitiser → I/Q demodulation.
  • Gate-based sensing and frequency multiplexing reduce hardware per qubit.
  • Reflectometry readout is the best match for the 4x2's capabilities.

Part III · Spin qubits · Chapter 10

An electron spin in a dot: Zeeman, spin-orbit, hyperfine and valleys

Why you need this

A spin qubit is not an isolated spin in vacuum. It lives in a crystal, inside an electrostatic trap, next to other electrons and (in some materials) millions of nuclear spins. Four interactions shape everything you will measure: the Zeeman effect (sets the qubit frequency), spin–orbit coupling (allows electric control and causes relaxation), the hyperfine interaction with nuclei (causes dephasing), and, in silicon, the valley degree of freedom. A fifth, the exchange interaction between neighbouring electrons, is what makes two-qubit gates and several qubit encodings possible. This chapter collects them in one place with their typical sizes.

10.1The energy ladder of a spin qubit device

Before going into each interaction, here are the energy scales of a typical Si/SiGe device, from largest to smallest. Keeping these in your head makes most papers easy to follow. Frequency equivalents use \(1\ \mu\text{eV} \leftrightarrow 0.242\) GHz.

EnergyTypical sizeFrequency equivalentWhat it controls
Charging energy \(E_C\)2–10 meV0.5–2.4 THzElectron number
Orbital spacing1–4 meV0.2–1 THzExcited orbital states
Valley splitting \(E_{VS}\)20–300 µeV5–70 GHzExtra low-lying states in Si
Zeeman splitting \(E_Z\)10–120 µeV (0.1–1 T)2.8–28 GHzQubit frequency
Tunnel coupling \(t_c\)0.1–100 µeV0.02–24 GHzExchange, PSB
Exchange \(J\)0–1 µeV (operational)0–250 MHzTwo-qubit gates
Thermal \(k_BT_e\) at 100 mK8.6 µeV2 GHzInitialisation, readout errors
Micromagnet field difference between dots~0.2–2 µeV50–500 MHzQubit addressability
Rabi frequency (as energy)~0.004–0.08 µeV1–20 MHzGate speed

10.2Zeeman effect and the g-factor

The Zeeman energy \(E_Z = g\mu_B B\) (Chapter 2) gives the qubit frequency. For electrons in silicon, \(g\) is very close to the free-electron value of 2.0023, because silicon's conduction band has weak spin–orbit coupling. It is not exactly 2: interface electric fields and the valley state shift \(g\) by parts in \(10^3\)–\(10^4\), and these shifts depend on gate voltages. This electrical tunability of \(g\) (a Stark shift) is small but useful: in Si-MOS devices it is used to address individual qubits, and it also means charge noise can shift the qubit frequency [7].

In GaAs, \(g\approx -0.44\), so a 1 T field gives only 6.2 GHz. Holes in germanium have g-factors that depend strongly on field direction, from about 0.1 in-plane to more than 10 out-of-plane, so the qubit frequency changes a lot if the sample is tilted in the magnet [12].

10.3Spin–orbit coupling

An electron moving through an electric field sees, in its own rest frame, an effective magnetic field. In a crystal, electric fields come from the crystal structure (inversion asymmetry of the lattice, giving the Dresselhaus term) and from the heterostructure and gates (structural asymmetry, giving the Rashba term). The result is a coupling between the electron's momentum and its spin, schematically

\[ H_{SO} = \alpha_R(\sigma_x k_y - \sigma_y k_x) + \beta_D(\sigma_x k_x - \sigma_y k_y) . \]

Its strength is often expressed as a spin–orbit length \(\ell_{SO}\): the distance an electron must travel for its spin to rotate by one radian. In GaAs \(\ell_{SO}\) is a few micrometres; in silicon conduction electrons it is much longer (weak coupling); in germanium holes it is short (strong coupling).

Spin–orbit coupling has two consequences for qubits:

  • It allows electric control. Shaking the electron back and forth with an oscillating gate voltage moves it in space; with spin–orbit coupling, that motion appears to the spin as an oscillating magnetic field. This is intrinsic electric-dipole spin resonance (EDSR). It works well in GaAs and germanium. In silicon electrons it is too weak, so a micromagnet provides an artificial, much stronger "spin–orbit" effect (Chapter 12).
  • It causes relaxation. It mixes spin and orbital states, letting phonons cause spin flips (Chapter 4).

10.4Hyperfine interaction with nuclear spins

An electron in a dot overlaps with many atomic nuclei. If those nuclei have spin, the electron feels their combined magnetic field through the hyperfine interaction, dominated by the Fermi contact term:

\[ H_{hf} = \sum_k A_k\,\vec S\cdot\vec I_k \;\approx\; g\mu_B\,\vec B_{\text{nuc}}\cdot\vec S . \]

The sum over \(k\) runs over all nuclei in the dot, with coupling \(A_k\) proportional to the electron density at nucleus \(k\). The total behaves like an extra random magnetic field, the Overhauser field \(\vec B_{\text{nuc}}\). Its average is zero, but its fluctuations are not: with \(N\) nuclei pointing randomly, the field fluctuates by an amount of order \(1/\sqrt N\) times the fully polarised field. The nuclear spins change slowly (milliseconds to seconds), so the Overhauser field looks quasi-static during a shot but different from shot to shot. This is exactly the noise that gives a Gaussian Ramsey decay (Chapter 4).

Worked example: GaAs dephasing time

In a GaAs dot of about \(10^6\) nuclei, the Overhauser field fluctuates with a standard deviation of roughly \(\sigma_B \approx 2\) mT [18]. The frequency spread is \(\sigma_\omega = |g|\mu_B\sigma_B/\hbar = 0.44\times9.27\times10^{-24}\times2\times10^{-3}/1.055\times10^{-34} \approx 7.7\times10^7\) rad/s. Then \(T_2^* = \sqrt2/\sigma_\omega \approx 18\) ns. This matches measured values of 10–20 ns [19].

In natural silicon only 4.7% of nuclei (29Si) carry spin, and the coupling per nucleus is weaker; \(T_2^*\) is around 1 µs. In isotopically purified 28Si with 800 ppm or less 29Si, hyperfine noise becomes negligible and charge noise takes over as the main dephasing source [13]. GaAs experiments, in turn, learned to use the nuclear field: singlet–triplet qubits in GaAs use a deliberately prepared Overhauser field difference between two dots as a control axis (Chapter 13), and real-time Bayesian estimation of the nuclear field has been used to extend coherence.

10.5Valleys again: spin–valley mixing

Chapter 6 introduced the two low-lying valley states in silicon, split by \(E_{VS}\). With spin, a single electron in the dot has four low-lying states: \(\ket{v_-,\downarrow}, \ket{v_-,\uparrow}, \ket{v_+,\downarrow}, \ket{v_+,\uparrow}\). As the magnetic field increases, \(\ket{v_-,\uparrow}\) moves up and \(\ket{v_+,\downarrow}\) moves down. They meet when \(E_Z = E_{VS}\). Spin–orbit coupling (and interface roughness) couples them weakly, producing an anticrossing.

Two practical lessons follow. Operate the qubit well away from the hot spot. And measure \(E_{VS}\) for every qubit dot, because it varies randomly from dot to dot in Si/SiGe. Measuring \(T_1\) versus \(B\) and locating the peak is one standard method [7].

10.6Two electrons: the exchange interaction

Two electrons in neighbouring dots interact through their wavefunctions' overlap. Because electrons are fermions, the total wavefunction must be antisymmetric. The spin singlet (antisymmetric in spin) must have a symmetric orbital part, and the triplets (symmetric in spin) an antisymmetric orbital part. These orbital parts have different energies, so the singlet and triplets split. The splitting \(J\) is the exchange energy, and the spin physics is described by the Heisenberg Hamiltonian

\[ H_{ex} = J\Big(\vec S_1\cdot\vec S_2 - \frac14\Big) \]

(with \(\vec S\) in units of \(\hbar\)), which gives energy \(-J\) to the singlet and 0 to the triplets.

In a double dot, \(J\) comes from virtual tunnelling: the electron in dot 1 can briefly hop to dot 2 and back, but only if the spins form a singlet (two electrons cannot share an orbital with parallel spin). Second-order perturbation theory in the Hubbard model gives

\[ J(\varepsilon) \approx \frac{2t_c^2}{U - \varepsilon} + \frac{2t_c^2}{U + \varepsilon} = \frac{4t_c^2\,U}{U^2 - \varepsilon^2} , \]

where \(U\) is the on-site charging energy and \(\varepsilon\) the detuning between the dots. This formula shows the two ways to turn exchange on:

  • Detuning control: increase \(|\varepsilon|\) towards \(U\), pushing one electron towards the other dot. Simple, but \(dJ/d\varepsilon\) is large, so charge noise in \(\varepsilon\) causes exchange noise.
  • Barrier (symmetric) control: keep \(\varepsilon = 0\), where \(dJ/d\varepsilon = 0\), and increase \(t_c\) by lowering the barrier gate. \(J\propto t_c^2\) and \(t_c\) depends exponentially on barrier voltage, so \(J\) can be switched over many orders of magnitude while staying first-order insensitive to detuning noise. Most modern experiments use barrier control [7].
Worked example: exchange in frequency units

With \(t_c = 10\ \mu\)eV, \(U = 3\) meV and \(\varepsilon = 0\): \(J = 4t_c^2/U = 4\times100/3000 = 0.133\ \mu\)eV, about 32 MHz. Lowering the barrier so that \(t_c\) doubles gives \(J\approx 0.53\ \mu\)eV ≈ 130 MHz. The HRL exchange-only experiments with spinQICK reached \(J/h\approx 75\)–78 MHz with 10 ns pulses [11]. So exchange pulses are short (ns) baseband voltage pulses of a few to tens of mV on barrier gates, which is a job for a fast DAC.

On the 4x2

Map each physical scale to the hardware that controls it:

  • Zeeman (GHz): microwave drive. Direct from the 4x2's DACs up to about 4.9 GHz (first Nyquist zone at 9.83 GSPS), or higher with an external mixer.
  • Exchange (MHz, ns pulses): baseband pulses on barrier gates. The 4x2 can produce short pulses (its sample time is 0.1 ns) but its outputs are AC-coupled, so pulses with a DC component droop (Chapter 29).
  • Charge transitions (detuning pulses, µs): baseband pulses on plungers, with the same AC-coupling issue.
  • Readout (sensor): reflectometry at 100 MHz–1 GHz, a perfect fit.
Check yourself

1. Why does purifying silicon to 28Si improve \(T_2^*\) so much, while purifying GaAs is impossible?

Show answer
28Si has nuclear spin zero, so removing 29Si removes almost all hyperfine noise. All stable isotopes of Ga and As have nuclear spin 3/2, so there is no spin-free GaAs.

2. Why is barrier-controlled ("symmetric") exchange less sensitive to charge noise?

Show answer
At \(\varepsilon = 0\), \(J(\varepsilon)\) is at a minimum with respect to detuning: \(dJ/d\varepsilon = 0\). Small detuning fluctuations change \(J\) only to second order. Changing \(J\) through \(t_c\) avoids moving away from this sweet spot.

3. A dot has \(E_{VS} = 150\ \mu\)eV. Up to roughly what field can you operate before hitting the hot spot?

Show answer
\(B = E_{VS}/(g\mu_B) = 150/115.8 \approx 1.3\) T, a qubit frequency of about 36 GHz. You would normally stay well below this.
Summary
  • Zeeman: \(E_Z = g\mu_B B\); \(g\approx2\) in Si (slightly gate-tunable), −0.44 in GaAs, anisotropic for holes.
  • Spin–orbit coupling enables intrinsic EDSR (GaAs, holes) and causes relaxation; it is weak for Si electrons, hence micromagnets.
  • Hyperfine coupling gives a quasi-static random Overhauser field: \(T_2^*\sim 10\) ns in GaAs, ~1 µs in natural Si, negligible in purified 28Si.
  • Silicon's valley splitting creates a relaxation hot spot at \(E_Z = E_{VS}\).
  • Exchange \(J \approx 4t_c^2U/(U^2-\varepsilon^2)\) is switched by detuning or (better) by barrier gates, using ns baseband pulses.

Part III · Spin qubits · Chapter 11

Spin readout: Elzerman, Pauli spin blockade and latching

Why you need this

The magnetic moment of one electron is far too small to detect directly. Every spin-qubit readout therefore converts spin into charge: "spin up" is made to move an electron somewhere, "spin down" is not (or vice versa), and the charge sensor from Chapter 9 sees the difference. There are two main conversion methods. Which one you use decides the pulse sequence, the required magnetic field and temperature, the readout time, and how much the RFSoC has to do in real time. This chapter explains both from the energy diagrams up.

11.1Spin-to-charge conversion

The idea is always the same: arrange the energy levels so that an electron (or a pair of electrons) can tunnel to a new position only for one spin state. Then measure the charge with the sensor. The spin information becomes a charge signal of the same size as any charge transition, which a good sensor reads in microseconds. The price is that readout destroys the spin state (it is "demolition" readout), and it takes far longer than gate operations (µs versus ns).

11.2Energy-selective (Elzerman) readout

The first single-shot readout of an electron spin, by Elzerman and colleagues in 2004, used one dot next to one reservoir [17]. In a magnetic field, the dot's single-electron level is split into \(E_\downarrow\) and \(E_\uparrow = E_\downarrow + E_Z\). The plunger voltage moves both levels together relative to the reservoir's Fermi level \(E_F\).

In the read phase, the charge sensor shows a short "blip" if the spin was up: the electron leaves (sensor signal changes) and a spin-down electron soon refills the dot (signal returns). If the spin was down, nothing happens. Detecting the blip with a threshold is single-shot readout.

Requirements and limitations

  • Zeeman energy well above the electron temperature. The Fermi level sits between \(E_\downarrow\) and \(E_\uparrow\). Thermal smearing of the reservoir lets a spin-down electron leave (false "up") or blocks a spin-up electron (false "down"). You need \(E_Z\) of at least several \(k_BT_e\): for \(T_e = 100\) mK that means \(E_Z\gtrsim 40\ \mu\)eV, so \(B\gtrsim 0.35\) T in silicon. This pushes the qubit frequency to 10 GHz and above.
  • Tunnel rate in the right window. The tunnel-out time must be longer than the sensor's response time (so blips are visible) and much shorter than \(T_1\) (so the spin does not relax before it is read). Typical tunnel times are 1–100 µs.
  • Long readout window. Because tunnelling is random, the read phase must last several tunnel times, typically 50 µs–1 ms. Elzerman readout is therefore slow compared with Pauli blockade.
  • Needs a reservoir next to the qubit dot. In long arrays, inner dots have no reservoir, so Elzerman readout only works at the ends.
In the lab

Energy-selective readout gives two other tools for free. Initialisation: in the load phase, place only \(E_\downarrow\) below \(E_F\), and only a spin-down electron can enter. T1 without control: load a random spin, wait, read; the fraction of blips versus wait time gives \(T_1\). These were how the first spin relaxation times in quantum dots were measured [17, 18].

11.3Pauli spin blockade (PSB)

Pauli spin blockade uses two electrons in two dots. Start in the \((1,1)\) charge state (one electron in each dot) and pulse the detuning towards \((2,0)\), where both electrons would sit in the left dot. Two electrons in the same dot's ground orbital must form a singlet, because the Pauli exclusion principle forbids two parallel spins in the same orbital (and the same valley). The triplet \((2,0)\) states require one electron in an excited orbital or valley state, which costs an extra energy \(E_{ST}\) (typically 0.1–1 meV in silicon, limited by the valley splitting).

So in a detuning window just past the \((1,1)\)–\((2,0)\) transition:

  • if the spins form a singlet, the right electron tunnels left and the charge becomes \((2,0)\);
  • if they form a triplet, tunnelling is blocked and the charge stays \((1,1)\).

The charge sensor distinguishes \((2,0)\) from \((1,1)\). Spin information has become charge information without needing a reservoir or a large Zeeman energy [18, 33].

What PSB actually measures

PSB distinguishes "singlet" from "triplet", but the details depend on the magnetic fields:

  • With a large Zeeman difference between the two dots (for example from a micromagnet gradient), \(T_0\) and \(S\) mix quickly in \((1,1)\). During readout, \(\ket{\uparrow\downarrow}\) and \(\ket{\downarrow\uparrow}\) both partly convert to singlet, so PSB measures the parity of the two spins: antiparallel (\(\uparrow\downarrow, \downarrow\uparrow\)) versus parallel (\(\uparrow\uparrow, \downarrow\downarrow\)). spinQICK calls this parity readout [10].
  • With a small field difference (and a well-chosen pulse), PSB measures singlet versus all triplets, as used in singlet–triplet qubits (Chapter 13).
  • Spin–orbit coupling can mix \(T_\pm\) with \(S\) and lift the blockade, especially in silicon at certain field directions [33]. Readout must be faster than this mixing.

To read a single qubit with PSB, pair it with a reference spin in a known state (for example spin down in the neighbouring dot). Then "parallel or antiparallel" tells you the qubit's state.

Why PSB is so widely used

  • It does not need a reservoir next to the qubit dot, so it works anywhere in an array.
  • It works at low magnetic fields and at higher temperatures (up to ~1 K), because it depends on \(E_{ST}\) (hundreds of µeV), not on \(E_Z\).
  • It is fast: the charge changes deterministically when you pulse (no waiting for random tunnelling), so readout time is set by the sensor's SNR. With RF reflectometry, single-shot PSB readout in a few microseconds is routine [32].

11.4Latching and shelving: making the signal bigger

The charge difference between \((2,0)\) and \((1,1)\) is just one electron moving by one dot spacing, which a sensor far away may barely see. Several enhancements map the two outcomes onto charge states that differ more strongly, or that are stable for longer:

  • Latched readout: arrange tunnel rates so that one outcome quickly proceeds to a different total-charge state (an electron enters or leaves from a reservoir), which then persists long after the spin would have relaxed. The sensor then measures a large, long-lived difference [34].
  • Shelving into metastable charge states serves the same purpose in larger arrays.

These tricks need extra pulse segments and careful timing of tunnel rates, again baseband voltage pulses on plungers.

11.5A readout timing budget

Worked example

Your reflectometry sensor has \(t_{\min} = 100\) ns (SNR 1 in 100 ns, Chapter 9). The triplet state relaxes to the singlet during readout with a time \(T_1^{\text{RO}} = 50\ \mu\)s. How long should you integrate?

For SNR 6 you need \(t = 36\,t_{\min} = 3.6\ \mu\)s. The probability that a triplet relaxes during that time is about \(3.6/50 \approx 7\%\), which would itself limit fidelity to roughly 96%. Integrating for 1.6 µs gives SNR 4 (2.3% overlap error each) and 3.2% relaxation error. The optimum is in between, and it is found experimentally by recording single-shot traces and analysing them offline or with an FPGA-based filter. This trade-off is why so much effort goes into faster sensors and amplifiers.

On the 4x2

Readout splits into two hardware tasks:

  • Reading the sensor: carrier generation, demodulation, integration and thresholding. This is what the 4x2 and QICK do well. QICK can return the integrated I/Q of every shot, or raw decimated traces for analysing blips and relaxation (Chapter 23).
  • Pulsing the plungers to the load, read and empty points (Elzerman), or across the interdot line (PSB). These are baseband pulses lasting µs (PSB) to ms (Elzerman). The 4x2's AC-coupled DAC outputs cannot hold these levels. You either use a separate DC-coupled AWG (triggered by the 4x2's PMOD outputs), modify the 4x2's output path, or use a board with DC-coupled outputs. spinQICK's PSB readout ran on a ZCU216 with DC-coupled amplifiers [11]. Chapter 38 compares the options.
Check yourself

1. Why does Elzerman readout need a large magnetic field while PSB does not?

Show answer
Elzerman readout discriminates spin by energy relative to the reservoir Fermi level, so \(E_Z\) must exceed the thermal smearing (several \(k_BT_e\)). PSB discriminates by the Pauli principle; the relevant energy is the singlet–triplet splitting of the doubly occupied dot (\(E_{ST}\), hundreds of µeV), which is independent of the field.

2. In a micromagnet device with a large field difference between two dots, PSB readout cannot distinguish \(\ket{\uparrow\downarrow}\) from \(\ket{\downarrow\uparrow}\). Why, and what does it measure?

Show answer
The field difference rapidly mixes \(S\) and \(T_0\) in (1,1), and both \(\ket{\uparrow\downarrow}\) and \(\ket{\downarrow\uparrow}\) are equal combinations of S and T₀. Both therefore unblock partially in the same way. PSB then measures parity: parallel spins (blocked) versus antiparallel (not blocked).

3. What limits how long the Elzerman read window must be?

Show answer
The tunnel-out time of the spin-up electron: you must wait several tunnel times to be sure an up spin has left. But the window must be short compared with \(T_1\), or up spins relax first and are misread as down.
Summary
  • Spin readout converts spin to charge and reads the charge with a sensor.
  • Elzerman readout: spin-up tunnels out to a reservoir; needs \(E_Z \gg k_BT_e\), a reservoir, and read windows of tens of µs to ms.
  • PSB: singlets move to (2,0), triplets are blocked; works anywhere in an array, at low field and higher temperature, and fast; measures singlet/triplet or parity.
  • Latching and shelving enhance the charge signal.
  • The 4x2 handles sensor readout well; the plunger pulses for readout need DC-coupled outputs.

Part III · Spin qubits · Chapter 12

Single-spin (Loss–DiVincenzo) qubits: ESR, EDSR and micromagnets

Why you need this

This is the qubit your device is built for: one electron spin per dot in Si/SiGe, rotated by microwaves applied to a gate, with a cobalt micromagnet converting electric motion into an effective magnetic drive. Understanding exactly how the micromagnet works tells you what microwave frequency and power you need, why the two qubits under one magnet have different frequencies, why charge noise dephases them, and what the RFSoC must generate. It also explains why your choice of magnetic field is really a choice of microwave hardware.

12.1The Loss–DiVincenzo qubit

Loss and DiVincenzo proposed in 1998 that the spin of a single electron in each quantum dot could serve as a qubit, with single-qubit gates from local magnetic fields and two-qubit gates from pulsed exchange between neighbouring dots [6]. Twenty-five years later this is the most widespread spin-qubit design: it is called the Loss–DiVincenzo (LD) qubit or single-spin qubit. Its operations map directly onto earlier chapters:

TaskHow it is doneChapter
Qubit states\(\ket\downarrow\), \(\ket\uparrow\) along the total field at the dot2, 10
InitialisationEnergy-selective loading of spin down, or via a \((2,0)\) singlet11
Single-qubit gatesESR or EDSR at the qubit frequency (this chapter)3, 12
Two-qubit gatesPulsed exchange \(J\)14
ReadoutElzerman or Pauli spin blockade + charge sensor9, 11

12.2Driving with a real oscillating magnetic field (ESR)

The textbook approach is electron spin resonance: send a microwave current through an on-chip wire (a stripline or antenna) near the dot, producing an oscillating magnetic field \(B_1\). From Chapter 3, the Rabi frequency is \(f_R = g\mu_B B_1/(2h)\) for a linearly polarised field (only the co-rotating half drives the spin). In silicon this is 14 MHz per mT.

ESR was first demonstrated for a single electron in a GaAs double dot in 2006 [35], and on-chip ESR antennas are used in Si-MOS devices. The drawbacks are practical: producing even 1 mT at the dot needs milliamperes of microwave current, which heats the device, and the field also creates electric fields that shake the electrons. Rabi frequencies are typically below 1 MHz.

12.3Driving with an electric field (EDSR)

Gates are much better at making electric fields than magnetic ones. Electric-dipole spin resonance applies a microwave voltage to a gate, which pushes the electron back and forth by a tiny distance. If the electron's spin is coupled to its position, that motion drives the spin. In GaAs and in germanium holes, intrinsic spin–orbit coupling provides this coupling (Chapter 10). In silicon electrons, spin–orbit coupling is weak, so a coupling is engineered with a magnetic field gradient [36, 37].

The micromagnet mechanism

Place a ferromagnet (usually cobalt) on top of the device. Its stray field \(\vec B_{\text{mm}}(\vec r)\) varies with position. Now shake the electron along x with amplitude \(x_{ac}\):

\[ x(t) = x_{ac}\cos\omega t \quad\Rightarrow\quad \vec B(t) \approx \vec B_{\text{mm}}(0) + \frac{\partial\vec B_{\text{mm}}}{\partial x}\,x_{ac}\cos\omega t . \]

Split the gradient into two parts relative to the total static field direction (call it z):

  • the transverse gradient \(b_\perp = \partial B_\perp/\partial x\) produces an oscillating field perpendicular to z. This is exactly the drive term of Chapter 3, with amplitude \(B_1 = b_\perp x_{ac}\).
  • the longitudinal gradient \(b_\parallel = \partial B_z/\partial x\) makes the qubit frequency depend on position. It does not drive the spin, but it makes different dots have different frequencies, and it converts electron motion from charge noise into frequency noise.

The Rabi frequency is

\[ f_R = \frac{g\mu_B}{2h}\,b_\perp\,x_{ac} . \]

How large is \(x_{ac}\)? For an electron in a harmonic confining potential of orbital energy \(\hbar\omega_{\text{orb}}\), an AC electric field \(E_{ac}\) displaces it by \(x_{ac} = eE_{ac}/(m^*\omega_{\text{orb}}^2)\). Softer confinement (smaller \(\omega_{\text{orb}}\)) means larger displacement and faster Rabi oscillations, but also more sensitivity to charge noise.

Worked example

A micromagnet gives \(b_\perp = 0.5\) mT/nm at the dot. You want \(f_R = 5\) MHz. What displacement is needed?

\(f_R = 14\ \text{MHz/mT}\times b_\perp x_{ac}\), so \(b_\perp x_{ac} = 5/14 = 0.36\) mT and \(x_{ac} = 0.36/0.5 \approx 0.7\) nm. The electron moves by less than a nanometre, a few percent of the dot size (tens of nm). The microwave amplitude needed at the gate to do this is typically around a millivolt to a few millivolts.

The design trade-off

The micromagnet must provide three things at once:

  1. Large transverse gradient \(b_\perp\) at each dot, for fast Rabi oscillations.
  2. Different longitudinal fields at neighbouring dots, so that each qubit has its own frequency and a microwave burst at one frequency rotates only one qubit. Typical separations are tens to hundreds of MHz.
  3. Small longitudinal gradient \(b_\parallel\) at each dot, so that electron jitter from charge noise does not change the qubit frequency much.

Points 2 and 3 conflict: the field must change between dots but be flat at each dot. Yoneda and colleagues designed a magnet that kept \(b_\parallel\) small at the qubit location, reaching \(T_2^*\approx 20\ \mu\)s and over 99.9% single-qubit fidelity in purified silicon [13]. The micromagnet must also be fully magnetised so its field is stable: cobalt micromagnets are usually operated with an in-plane external field of several hundred millitesla, which puts the qubit frequency around 10–20 GHz.

12.4Spectroscopy and addressing several qubits

A device with two qubits under one micromagnet shows two EDSR lines. Their frequencies are \(f_{1,2} = g\mu_B(B_0 + B_{\text{mm},1,2})/h\). Each qubit is addressed by driving at its own frequency, often through the same gate. Several practical issues appear:

  • Crosstalk: a strong drive at \(f_1\) slightly rotates qubit 2 if \(f_2 - f_1\) is not large compared with the Rabi frequency. Smooth pulse envelopes (Chapter 3) and frequency separation reduce this.
  • AC Stark shifts: driving qubit 1 shifts qubit 2's frequency, leading to phase errors on qubit 2. They are calibrated and compensated with virtual Z rotations [14].
  • Microwave-induced heating: in several silicon devices, applying microwaves shifts qubit frequencies by tens of kHz to MHz, apparently through heating. Groups keep the total microwave power constant over time, for example with off-resonant "dummy" pulses [16].

12.5Other single-spin drive methods

  • Intrinsic spin–orbit EDSR in GaAs and in germanium holes, with no micromagnet. Hole qubits in germanium reach Rabi frequencies of tens of MHz this way [12].
  • g-tensor modulation: a gate voltage changes the g-factor's direction or size, which drives the spin. Important for holes and some Si-MOS devices.
  • Flopping-mode EDSR: drive an electron between two dots near the interdot transition, so that it moves a large distance through the gradient. This gives fast Rabi frequencies at low microwave power, at the cost of more charge-noise sensitivity [7].
In the lab

The microwave reaches the device through a dedicated attenuated coaxial line, often combined with the DC voltage of a gate in a bias tee on the sample PCB. Typical source powers are −10 to +10 dBm at room temperature with 20–40 dB of attenuation in the fridge, so the gate sees roughly −30 to −50 dBm (about 1–10 mV amplitude across 50 Ω). Groups tune the power by watching the Rabi frequency, which should rise linearly with drive amplitude until heating or nonlinear effects appear.

On the 4x2

EDSR is where the frequency plan meets your magnet:

  • Direct synthesis, first Nyquist zone (up to about 4.9 GHz): needs the total field at the dot to be below about 0.175 T. A cobalt micromagnet may not be fully magnetised at such low external fields, and readout by Elzerman would be thermally limited. Possible, but not the usual operating point.
  • Second Nyquist zone (about 4.9–9.8 GHz): QICK lets a generator use the DAC's second Nyquist zone (nqz=2). Output power falls with frequency because of the DAC's sinc roll-off and analog bandwidth, so check the actual power with a spectrum analyser. This reaches fields of roughly 0.18–0.35 T.
  • External upconversion (any frequency): generate an intermediate frequency (IF) of a few hundred MHz to ~1–2 GHz on one DAC, mix it with a local oscillator (LO) from a separate microwave source, and filter out the unwanted sideband. With two DACs you can feed the I and Q inputs of an IQ mixer for clean single-sideband output, but that uses both outputs and leaves none for readout. Chapter 20 explains the trade-offs, and Chapter 42 gives a full EDSR setup.

Because the 4x2's DACs are AC-coupled, they are fine for microwave bursts, which have no DC component. Microwave drive is a natural job for the board.

Check yourself

1. Two qubits sit 100 nm apart under a micromagnet whose longitudinal field changes by 0.2 mT/nm between them. What is their frequency difference?

Show answer
\(\Delta B_z = 0.2\times100 = 20\) mT, so \(\Delta f = 28\ \text{GHz/T}\times0.02\ \text{T} = 560\) MHz (if the gradient were uniform; real field profiles are not, but the order of magnitude is typical).

2. Why does a larger longitudinal gradient at the dot reduce \(T_2^*\)?

Show answer
Charge noise moves the electron slightly. With a longitudinal gradient, position fluctuations become qubit-frequency fluctuations, \(\delta f = (g\mu_B/h)\,b_\parallel\,\delta x\), which dephase the qubit.

3. Your qubit is at 13.2 GHz. Can the 4x2 drive it directly?

Show answer
Not directly in the first or second Nyquist zone at 9.83 GSPS (above about 9.8 GHz is the third zone, with very low power and above the balun rating). Use an external LO and mixer: for example, an LO at 12 GHz and a 1.2 GHz IF from one DAC, with a filter to remove the 10.8 GHz image.
Summary
  • LD qubits use one electron spin per dot, ESR/EDSR for single-qubit gates, exchange for two-qubit gates, and spin-to-charge readout.
  • ESR uses a real oscillating magnetic field; EDSR shakes the electron electrically and needs spin–orbit coupling or a field gradient.
  • With a micromagnet, \(f_R = (g\mu_B/2h)\,b_\perp x_{ac}\); the longitudinal field difference separates qubit frequencies; the longitudinal gradient at each dot adds charge-noise dephasing.
  • Co micromagnets are usually operated at several hundred mT, putting qubit frequencies at 10–20 GHz, which requires external upconversion with the 4x2.
